{{Short description|Type of category in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''elementary topos''' (plural ''toposes'' or ''topoi''{{sfn|Johnstone|2014|p=xx}}) is a [[Category (mathematics)|category]] which has properties making it resemble the [[category of sets]]. Elementary toposes can be used as [[Model (mathematical logic)|model]]s of [[Intuitionistic logic|intuitionistic]] [[higher-order logic]].

== Introduction ==

An elementary topos (hereafter just topos) can be pictured as an alternate mathematical universe.{{r|blechschmidt}} It is a category which is sufficiently like the category of sets (the “standard mathematical universe”) that common mathematical constructions can be carried in it, such as subsets, [[function space]]s, etc.

More precisely, a topos supports [[Intuitionistic logic|intuitionistic]] [[higher-order logic]] as an [[internal language]]{{sfn|Lambek|Scott|1986|loc=part II}}. As such, toposes are widely used as models of [[constructive mathematics]].

== Definition ==

As originally defined by [[William Lawvere|Lawvere]] and [[Myles Tierney|Tierney]], an elementary topos is a category <math>\mathcal{E}</math> such that:{{sfn|Goldblatt|1984|p=84}}{{sfn|Johnstone|2002a|p=85}}

* <math>\mathcal{E}</math> is [[Finitely complete category|finitely complete]] (it has all finite [[Limit (category theory)|limits]]). Equivalently, it has a [[terminal object]], [[Binary product (category theory)|binary products]], and [[Equalizer (mathematics)#In category theory|binary equalizers]].
* <math>\mathcal{E}</math> is [[Finitely cocomplete category|finitely cocomplete]] (it has all finite [[Colimit (category theory)|colimits]]). Equivalently, it has an [[initial object]], binary [[Coproduct (category theory)|coproducts]] and binary [[coequalizer]]s.
* <math>\mathcal{E}</math> has [[exponential object]]s (in addition to binary products, which are required for defining exponential objects). Together with having a terminal object and binary products, this means that <math>\mathcal{E}</math> is [[Cartesian closed category|Cartesian closed]].
* <math>\mathcal{E}</math> has a [[subobject classifier]].

The requirement that <math>\mathcal{E}</math> be finitely cocomplete was later observed to be redundant, as it follows from the rest.{{sfn|Johnstone|2002a|loc=section A2.2}}{{sfn|van Oosten|2024|loc=section 3.2}}{{sfn|MacLane|Moerdijk|2012|loc=section IV.5}} (However, the general construction of finite colimits is relatively complicated; in most examples, one can find a more concrete description, which simplifies the translation of statements from the internal language.)

An even more minimalistic definition is possible: an elementary topos is a [[finitely complete category]] with [[power object]]s.{{sfn|Johnstone|2002a|p=92}} (This essentially replaces the requirements to have exponentials <math>A^B</math> and a subobject classifier <math>\Omega</math> with just the special case of exponentials <math>\Omega^B</math>.)

Many other properties follow, such as being [[Regular category|regular]] and moreover [[Regular category#Exact (effective) categories|exact]]{{sfn|Johnstone|2014|p=41}}{{sfn|van Oosten|2024|p=45}}.

== Logical functors ==

A ''logical functor'' is a functor between topoi that preserves finite limits and power objects. Logical functors preserve the structures that topoi have. In particular, they preserve finite colimits, [[subobject classifier]]s, and [[exponential object]]s.<ref name="McLarty1992">{{harvnb|McLarty|1992|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=V8cON1x39bIC&dq=%22Logical+functor%22 159]}}</ref>

== Examples ==

Having a subobject classifier is a strong requirement, which rules out most categories of algebraic structures such as [[Group (mathematics)|groups]], [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]], etc.{{r|catdat-subobject-classifier}}

Every [[Grothendieck topos]] (a category equivalent to the category of sheaves on a [[Site (mathematics)|site]]) is an elementary topos. Important special cases include:
* For any [[small category]] <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, the [[presheaf category]] <math>\operatorname{Set}^{\mathcal{C}^\operatorname{op}}</math>.
* As a further special case of the previous example, for any [[Group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math>, the category of <math>G</math>-sets, i.e., sets equipped with an [[Group action (mathematics)|action]] of <math>G</math>, with equivariant maps as morphisms.
* For any [[topological space]] <math>X</math>, the category of [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]] on <math>X</math>.
* The [[classifying topos]] for a geometric theory.

The category of finite sets is an elementary topos{{sfn|MacLane|Moerdijk|2012|p=27}} (however, it lacks a [[natural numbers object]]), and similarly for finite <math>G</math>-sets.

The [[effective topos]] is an important example of an elementary topos with natural numbers object. It is not a Grothendieck topos.{{r|van-oosten-effective-topos-not-grothendieck}} It can be viewed as a universe of [[Computability theory|computable]] mathematics. This example is generalized by [[realizability topos]]es.

A source of examples is the [[fundamental theorem of topos theory]], which states that for every elementary topos <math>\mathcal{E}</math> and every object <math>\Gamma \in \mathcal{E}</math>, the [[slice category]] <math>\mathcal{E}/\Gamma</math> is an elementary topos.
